title: [Research progress on early biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease].
journal: Zhonghua yu fang yi xue za zhi [Chinese journal of preventive medicine]
abstract: As the global population continues to age, Alzheimer's disease (AD) has become a serious public health issue. Compared to traditional diagnostic methods, blood biomarkers offer new avenues for early AD screening due to their advantages, such as low invasiveness and high throughput. In 2024, the National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) updated its ATN biomarker research framework, in which A, T, and N denote β-amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration (hereafter the ATN framework), formally establishing the diagnostic status of blood biomarkers and proposing Core 1 and Core 2 biomarkers for disease diagnosis and pathological staging; and atypical biomarkers, such as those related to neurodegeneration, inflammation, vascular damage, and comorbid proteins, to reflect mixed pathological states. Although these markers show substantial potential for early AD screening, their clinical translation is still limited by insufficient standardisation across assay platforms and by assay interference. This review summarises recent advances in early AD biomarkers and outlines the challenges and prospects for their translation.

title: Toll-Like Receptor-Driven Neuroinflammation in Neurological Disorders: Signaling Crosstalk and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) serve as pivotal mediators bridging innate immunity and neuroinflammation, orchestrating pathological cascades that drive neurological disorders. Beyond their sentinel role in pathogen recognition, aberrant TLR activation triggers intricate and destructive signaling networks, including activation of NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT, alongside IRFs and type I interferon responses that converge on chronic neuroinflammation and subsequent neuronal damage. This review dissects TLRs' multilayered contribution to neuropathology, emphasizing their regulation of secondary inflammatory mechanisms, including NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation, mTOR-driven metabolic dysregulation, SOCS-mediated feedback inhibition, inflammasome activation, and pyroptotic cell death. Critically, these signaling pathways create a pathological intersection with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, amplifying a self-perpetuating cycle of neuronal injury that underlies conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Stroke, Multiple sclerosis (MS), Epilepsy and Traumatic brain injury (TBI). Against this neuropathological landscape, this review systematically evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies targeting TLR-mediated neuroinflammation, encompassing small molecule TLR antagonists, intracellular adaptor protein inhibitors targeting myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) and TIR-domain-containing adapter-inducing interferon-β (TRIF), biologic therapies including monoclonal antibodies and fusion proteins, natural phytochemicals and nutraceuticals, Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genomic interventions, and cell-based immunomodulatory therapies, collectively representing a mechanistically diverse arsenal aimed at recalibrating the dysregulated innate immune response to achieve durable neuroprotection across the full spectrum of TLR-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons. Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons. Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it. Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.Significance Statement Foods typically present a complex mixture of tastes. However, understanding how the nervous system processes gustatory signals has traditionally relied on investigations that analyze responses to individual tastes. Our study investigates how mixtures of naturally occurring food tastes activate sensory neurons and how emergent signals arise when combinations of gustatory stimuli excite taste buds. Using in vivo imaging of primary gustatory neurons in mice, we show that sour stimuli suppress neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty tastes. The findings reveal an early, peripheral stage of neural computation that helps explain how complex flavors are encoded.

title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5-20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

title: HDAC1 modulates BAP1 acetylation and is associated with HIF-1α stabilization in brain injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage.
abstract: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a devastating cerebrovascular disease in which early brain injury is a major determinant of poor outcomes. Histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) is an important epigenetic regulator, yet its role in early brain injury after SAH remains poorly defined. Here, we investigated the function and mechanism of HDAC1 in SAH-induced early brain injury using in vivo and in vitro models. We found that HDAC1 expression was markedly upregulated after SAH and was primarily associated with neurons. HDAC1 inhibition significantly improved neurological function, reduced brain edema and blood-brain barrier disruption, and attenuated oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and neuronal apoptosis in SAH mice. Mechanistically, HDAC1 interacted with BAP1 and modulated its acetylation status, which was associated with enhanced BAP1 stability. Stabilized BAP1 further deubiquitinated and upregulated HIF-1α. In vivo, BAP1 knockdown similarly attenuated SAH-induced early brain injury. Moreover, BAP1 knockdown reduced OxyHb-induced oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis in vitro, whereas HIF-1α overexpression reversed these protective effects. Collectively, this study demonstrates that HDAC1 participates in the regulation of BAP1 acetylation status and stability, as well as subsequent HIF-1α deubiquitination, thereby contributing to early brain injury after SAH, and suggests that the HDAC1/BAP1/HIF-1α axis may serve as a potential therapeutic target for early intervention in SAH.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Behavioral Phenotyping: From Behavioral Neuroscience to Depression Research.
abstract: Behavioral phenotyping remains the main experimental readout for investigating brain function and neuropsychiatric disease. However, conventional behavioral analysis relies largely on manually defined endpoints that simplify the multidimensional nature of behavior and often overlook subtle behavioral dynamics. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL) and computer vision, are fundamentally transforming this landscape by enabling automated, high-resolution quantification of behavior across species and experimental paradigms. This review discusses recent developments in AI-based behavioral phenotyping and their implications for translational neuroscience, with particular emphasis on emerging applications to depression research. We first describe how markerless pose estimation has changed movement quantification, followed by supervised and unsupervised ML approaches that classify predefined behaviors or discover latent behavioral motifs directly from movement data. We then discuss how these approaches are reshaping systems neuroscience by enabling increasingly detailed descriptions of behavioral organization and facilitating the investigation of behavior as a continuous, multidimensional process. Finally, we examine their application to experimental models and clinical studies of depression, considering their potential and the limitations of translating computational behavioral measures across experimental and clinical settings. AI-based behavioral phenotyping represents an important methodological advance in neuroscience, shifting behavioral analysis from the quantification of isolated experimental endpoints toward the characterization of integrated behavioral states. In depression research, these approaches may improve behavioral characterization in experimental models and provide quantitative measures of clinically-relevant behavioral alterations in humans. However, linking experimental and clinical phenotypes will require methodological standardization, independent validation, and careful evaluation of cross-species comparability.

title: The disrupted navigational compass: pathophysiological mechanisms and clinical interventions for spatial navigation deficits.
abstract: Spatial navigation is a higher-order integrative cognitive ability that supports environmental orientation, goal-directed route selection, and adaptive locomotion by integrating spatial memory, multisensory cues, attention, and executive control. Neural systems supporting navigation are also vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease, making navigation a useful domain for linking basic mechanisms with clinically measurable functional impairment. This review summarizes spatial-navigation mechanisms across multiple levels. At the cognitive level, navigation depends on interacting processes including spatial representation, path integration, reference-frame transformation, landmark use, and route planning. At the network level, hippocampal-entorhinal, retrosplenial-parietal, scene-selective, and prefrontal systems contribute complementary functions. At the cellular level, place-, grid-, head-direction-, speed-, and boundary-related representations encode position, heading, self-motion, environmental geometry, and prospective behavior. Clinical and neuroimaging studies indicate that navigation impairment is associated with structural and functional abnormalities, with the strongest diagnostic evidence currently arising from Alzheimer's disease and its prodromal stages. VR-based behavioral assessment and electrophysiological approaches provide complementary means of characterizing navigation phenotypes: VR enables controlled, repeatable, process-sensitive tasks, whereas intracranial and scalp recordings provide neural information at different spatial and physiological scales. No pharmacological agent has been developed or licensed specifically for navigation impairment; current navigation-focused interventions therefore rely mainly on behavioral and VR-based rehabilitation, compensatory strategies, and emerging neuromodulation approaches. Future studies should integrate process-specific behavioral and physiological markers with biomarker-defined clinical cohorts, and use large, randomized, longitudinal studies to establish diagnostic validity, real-world transfer, and mechanism-informed intervention effects.

title: System-level nonequivalence between integrated information and expected free energy in noisy permutation networks.
abstract: The free-energy principle (FEP) and active inference describe prediction and adaptation using generative models, whereas integrated information theory (IIT) examines intrinsic causal organization. Can knowledge of a network's prediction in its current state determine its intrinsic integration? We address this question using a fixed one-step state-risk expected free energy (EFE) and IIT system integrated information. Noisy binary permutation networks allow causal wiring to vary while local transition reliability remains fixed. From a homogeneous current state, different architectures have identical complete one-step predictive distributions, and thus identical EFE under common preferences and observation models. Nevertheless, multicycle architectures have zero whole-system IIT integration, while single cycles can be integrated. For an n-unit noisy single cycle with reliability η, we obtain the exact expression φsnη=min{2ηnlog22η,-nlog2η}. We prove that the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, establish a unique interior maximum, and show that, in the large-n limit, the optimal reliability approaches unity, the joint specified-state probability approaches one half, and the maximum system integrated information approaches one ibit. Independent computation corroborates these results. Local surprisal-coordinate identities can be expressed through optimized variational free energy under exact inference, but this algebraic identity does not establish that a neural system performs variational inference. The counterexample establishes a state-conditioned non-identifiability limit for the specified EFE, not an incompatibility between IIT and the FEP. Bridging the two descriptions requires intervention-sensitive information beyond this single predictive distribution.

title: Thickness of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer and its association with disease severity in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional case-control study.
abstract: Peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (pRNFL) alterations are linked to retinal neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease (PD), but their regional pattern and clinical relevance remain unclear. This cross-sectional case-control study included 63 PD patients (123 eyes; Hoehn-Yahr [H-Y] stages 1.0-2.5: 47; stages 3-5: 16) and 16 healthy controls (32 eyes). Swept-source optical coherence tomography measured average and quadrant-specific pRNFL thickness. Generalized estimating equations accounted for inter-eye correlation; Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) within each retinal parameter. Mean pRNFL thickness (prespecified primary outcome) was lower in PD than in controls (107.3 ± 10.9 vs. 112.8 ± 9.4 μm; p = 0.022). The age- and sex-adjusted difference persisted (-6.76 μm; p = 0.005), whereas the moderate-to-advanced versus early-stage difference was nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction (p = 0.148). Temporal pRNFL was thinner (exploratory, unadjusted p = 0.010). In unadjusted models, mean pRNFL thickness was negatively associated with H-Y stage, disease duration, and MDS-UPDRS total, Part II, and Part III scores (all q < 0.01). These associations persisted after adjustment, as did associations of inferior and temporal pRNFL with motor scores (all q < 0.05). No non-motor associations survived FDR correction. Exploratory participant-level ROC analyses yielded AUCs of 0.717 for H-Y stage ≥ 3 (mean pRNFL), 0.727 for MDS-UPDRS Part III ≥ 40 (temporal pRNFL), and 0.681 for PD versus controls (temporal pRNFL). These exploratory findings suggest regionally heterogeneous pRNFL involvement and support pRNFL as a non-invasive candidate marker of retinal neurodegeneration and clinical severity, but not a stand-alone diagnostic biomarker.

title: Association of scan time with resting-state functional connectivity discriminability: effects of temporal alignment.
abstract: Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is increasingly used to probe individual differences in brain organization, but individual-level FC discriminability may vary across repeated acquisitions related to arousal, physiology, and endogenous brain state. Acquisition-time variation may be a systematic contributor to this variability, yet its impact on FC discriminability has not been well characterized. Multi-session resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project were analyzed using minimally preprocessed and ICA-FIX-denoised BOLD time series. Whole-brain and network-level FC matrices were constructed after atlas-based parcellation, and sessions were grouped into one-hour daytime bins. Discriminability was computed to quantify how well repeated FC profiles from the same individual could be distinguished from those of other individuals, and grouped versus ungrouped estimates were compared. Temporal alignment of scans according to acquisition time substantially improved FC discriminability across both test-retest configurations. Whole-brain discriminability increased from 0.29 to 0.61 in one configuration and from 0.31 to 0.60 in the other. Similar gains were observed across canonical networks, with robust improvements in the default mode, dorsal attention, frontoparietal, and visual networks. These findings show that acquisition-time grouping was associated with higher FC discriminability in this HCP sample. Incorporating acquisition-time structure into rs-fMRI acquisition and analysis may enhance connectome fingerprinting and improve FC discriminability.

title: The challenge of Adenomyosis across the ART journey: insights from the Naples Workshop group.
abstract: Adenomyosis is increasingly recognized in women of reproductive age and may adversely affect fertility, assisted reproductive technology (ART) outcomes, and pregnancy. However, its optimal management in women seeking pregnancy remains uncertain, with substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria, disease phenotypes, and available therapeutic evidence. This narrative review, informed by the multidisciplinary discussion of the Naples Workshop on Adenomyosis and ART (10th-12th October 2025), critically examines the available evidence on adenomyosis throughout the ART journey. Available evidence is critically synthesized, with multidisciplinary clinical perspectives incorporated where appropriate, to identify practical clinical considerations, areas of uncertainty, and priorities for future research. The review is structured into three sections according to the phase of adenomyosis management during the ART timeline: (i) before ART, including diagnosis, ovarian reserve assessment and potential pre-treatment; (ii) during ART, including embryo transfer strategies; (iii) after ART, addressing pregnancy-related risks, antenatal surveillance, delivery, and postpartum management. This expert narrative review integrates available evidence with multidisciplinary clinical expertise to provide practical considerations for patient management while identifying areas of uncertainty and priorities for future research. Overall, management should be individualized according to disease phenotype, symptoms, reproductive potential, previous ART history, and coexisting conditions, while several commonly proposed interventions still require confirmation in well-designed prospective studies.

title: Down-regulation of circular RNA MBNL1 inhibits monocytic activation to alleviate depressive-like behaviors in mice.
abstract: Clinical studies have reported that elevated inflammatory markers are closely associated with the development of stress-related disorders, such as major depressive disorder (MDD), although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have been reported to be associated with MDD. The present study reveals that circMBNL1 expression is significantly upregulated in both plasma and monocytes from patients with MDD and positively correlates with the severity of depressive symptoms. We demonstrate that circMBNL1 drives pro-inflammatory activation of monocytes and promotes their infiltration into the brains of mice subjected to chronic unpredictable stress (CUS), thereby exacerbating neuroinflammation. Notably, extracellular vesicle (EV)-delivered sicircMBNL1 specifically downregulates circMBNL1 expression in peripheral monocytes, thereby attenuating Ly6Chi monocyte infiltration, preserving blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, suppressing microglial activation, restoring astrocytic function, and ultimately alleviating depressive-like behaviors in mice. Mechanistic investigations demonstrate that circMBNL1 knockdown induces ubiquitin-mediated degradation of the transcription factor STAT3, leading to downregulation of placental growth factor (PGF) expression and consequent suppression of monocyte activation. Our findings provide the first evidence implicating the circMBNL1-STAT3-PGF axis as a key mediator of neuroinflammatory processes in MDD, opening new avenues for developing targeted therapeutic strategies for depression.

title: Serotonergic, Dopaminergic, and Noradrenergic Modulation of Fear Extinction Memory.
abstract: Fear extinction is a key mechanism underlying exposure-based therapies, yet its neurobiological regulation remains only partially understood, limiting our ability to optimize treatment efficacy and durability in anxiety-related disorders. Serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine influence the amygdala, hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex, regulating neuronal excitability and the consolidation and retrieval of extinction memory. Most reviews have treated these systems separately or focused on a single phase of extinction, and few have asked how they interact across acquisition, consolidation, retrieval, and relapse. This review first synthesizes rodent evidence on serotonergic, dopaminergic, and noradrenergic modulation of fear extinction across its phases, examining their distinct contributions and the limited evidence for interactions among them. It then examines the convergence of these preclinical findings with clinical data and discusses the translational implications. We propose "monoamine-dependent adaptive plasticity" as a working hypothesis in which serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine make distinct, potentially interacting contributions to extinction-related plasticity. Within this tentative framework, dopamine is proposed to signal the omission of the expected aversive outcome, norepinephrine is implicated in setting the arousal and salience state for encoding the extinction context, and serotonin is suggested to modulate the balance between plasticity and generalization. We distinguish rodent, healthy-human, and clinical evidence and treat them as non-interchangeable levels of support, and convergence is partial and, in some cases, absent. By organizing the evidence around extinction phases rather than individual transmitters, this framework may help identify which mechanisms are most likely to translate into effective interventions.

title: Spatial coupling between anosmia-related cortical alterations and regional gene expression: an imaging transcriptomics study.
abstract: The impact of anosmia on brain cortical structure and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated causal associations between anosmia and cortical alterations using a multi-modal approach combining neuroimaging and genetics. High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging was acquired from 52 patients with anosmia and 50 healthy controls to extract cortical surface area (SA) and cortical thickness (TH). Mendelian randomization (MR) was employed to assess the causal effect of anosmia on cortical structure using summary statistics from the ENIGMA consortium. Furthermore, integrating gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), partial least squares regression (PLSR) and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) were used to identify genes associated with changes in SA and TH due to anosmia. Gene enrichment analysis and cell type-specific analysis were then performed to explore the potential molecular mechanisms. Patients exhibited significantly reduced SA in the left rostral anterior cingulate and superior temporal sulcus, while TH was increased in regions including the left cuneus and supramarginal gyrus. MR analysis identified 11 cortical structural features nominally associated with anosmia, although none survived multiple comparison correction across 138 tests. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes correlated with these structural alterations, which were significantly enriched in synaptic pathways (e.g., postsynaptic membrane modulation) and specifically implicated GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. Anosmia is causally associated with distinct cortical structural alterations. These regional changes are spatially coupled with molecular signatures involving synaptic function and neuronal plasticity, providing novel insights into the potential pathophysiology of olfactory loss.

title: Electromyography of the Tongue in Mechanically Ventilated Patients with Acute Brain Injury and Healthy Volunteers.
abstract: Assessment of upper airway function in ventilated patients with acute brain injury is important for extubation but limited by impaired consciousness and the endotracheal tube. As a marker of upper airway function, we investigated tongue electromyography (EMG) in healthy controls and mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury. In healthy participants, non-invasive tongue EMG was recorded during rest, deep breathing (nasal and oral), partially obstructed nasal breathing, and voluntary motor activation through pressing the tongue laterally against the molar teeth. In patients, EMG was recorded at baseline and during individualised physiological challenges involving modifications to ventilatory or oxygen support to increase upper airway stress. Follow-up recordings were obtained in six patients 2-4 days after baseline. External hypoglossal nerve stimulation yielded Compound Muscle Action Potentials (CMAPs). We define Glossal Function Index (GFI; EMG - CMAP Area-Under-Curve (AUC) ratio) and Rhythmic Involuntary Frequency (RIF) i.e., rate of prominent EMG peaks. We recruited 10 healthy participants and 10 patients. Taking the mean over 5 readings per participant, CMAP-AUC had median value 25 mVms (IQR 19-31 mVms) for healthy participants, and 12 mVms (IQR 9-15 mVms) amongst patients. Voluntary motor activation of the tongue yielded the highest median healthy-participant GFI (79 (IQR 53-90); other manoeuvres: 8 (IQR 5-19)). RIF demonstrated consistent rhythmic activity in healthy participants (median 13.4 peaks/min (IQR 11.2-14.9 peaks/min); 2/60 readings aperiodic). Patients frequently demonstrated irregular or arhythmic activity (median 8.5 peaks/min (IQR 8.1-10.1 peaks/min); 8/25 readings aperiodic). RIF matches EMG morphology of patients with frequent isolated bursts and greater periodicity during ventilator challenge and follow-up. Non-invasive tongue EMG characterised upper airway muscle activity in healthy individuals and ventilated patients with acute brain injury; GFI and RIF are novel markers for further evaluation in predicting extubation success.

title: Transcriptomic and behavioral analyses link perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) exposure to circadian and visual pathway disruption in larval zebrafish (Danio rerio).
abstract: Perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) is a short-chain perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) detected in fish tissues and environmental matrices, yet its mechanisms of toxicity remain poorly understood. We evaluated developmental, behavioral, and transcriptomic responses in zebrafish (Danio rerio) exposed to 0.1-100µg/L PFBA for seven days. Survival remained above 96%, although a slight reduction (~2%) was observed in exposed groups. Hatching rate and reactive oxygen species levels were unaffected. Behavioral analysis revealed hypoactivity at 0.1 and 1µg/L, restricted to the first dark and first light periods, indicating a non-monotonic concentration-response. RNA-seq identified 3,177, 1,919, and 2,277 differentially expressed transcripts at 0.1, 1, and 10µg/L, respectively. Exposure to 1µg/L altered circadian rhythm and photoperiodism pathways, whereas 10µg/L affected the nervous system, visual perception, and lens development. Circadian-related genes (cry2, cry3b, cryba1a) were differentially expressed, supporting transcriptomic findings and providing mechanistic insight into PFBA-induced behavioral alterations.

title: Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
journal: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology
abstract: Suicide is a leading, preventable cause of premature mortality, yet identifying individuals at imminent risk remains difficult. There are no validated biomarkers for routine stratification, and common approaches (clinical interviews, rating scales, self-report) are limited by subjectivity, reporting bias, and weak positive predictive value for rare outcomes. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning, deep learning, and large language models-offer opportunities to integrate heterogeneous signals relevant to risk and treatment response. This narrative review summarizes recent AI-enabled prediction and characterization of suicidal thoughts and behaviors across major data modalities: structured electronic health records and claims; natural language processing of clinical notes and digital text; speech and facial/behavioral signals; neuroimaging and other neurobiological measures; and passive sensing from smartphones and wearables. We review common modeling and evaluation practices, emphasizing clinically relevant performance assessment (discrimination and calibration) and the importance of temporal and external validation. We also highlight barriers to translation, including class imbalance and label noise, dataset shift across sites and time, limited prospective evaluation, and the need for interpretable outputs that can support medication decisions and care pathways (e.g., triage, monitoring, and stepped interventions). Ethical and implementation challenges-privacy and consent, algorithmic bias and equity, governance, and the clinical consequences of false-positive and false-negative predictions-are discussed with an emphasis on safe deployment. We conclude with priorities for the field, including multimodal longitudinal cohorts, harmonized reporting standards, and pragmatic trials to determine whether AI decision support measurably improves suicide-prevention outcomes.

title: Rotigotine Behenate ameliorates depression in Parkinson's disease through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection.
abstract: Depression in Parkinson's disease (DPD) is a prevalent non-motor complication that currently lacks effective targeted therapy. We established a combined MPTP/CUMS model in male C57BL/6 mice, which induced a higher incidence of depression and more stable depressive-like phenotypes than MPTP-only modeling and closely recapitulated clinical DPD pathology. Pearson correlation analysis confirmed severe dopamine (DA) and 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) dysregulation predominantly in the striatum (STR) and prefrontal cortex (PFC), identifying these regions as core DPD lesion sites. Behavioral assays demonstrated that ROTB ameliorated both motor dysfunction and depressive-like behavior and restored regional neurotransmitter balance, whereas fluoxetine-included solely as an efficacy comparator for the depressive-like phenotype-did not improve motor symptoms. Mechanistically, ROTB suppressed NF-κB/NLRP3-mediated neuroinflammation and activated the BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β cascade, elevating synaptic protein levels and reversing dendritic spine loss. Pharmacological inhibition of the NF-κB pathway with QNZ only partially recapitulated the antidepressant effects of ROTB, indicating the existence of NF-κB-independent protective mechanisms. In summary, ROTB alleviates DPD through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection, offering preclinical evidence for DPD therapy.

title: Hypoglossal-facial nerve anastomosis for facial nerve injury after vestibular schwannoma surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
abstract: Facial nerve injury is one of the most common and distressing complications following vestibular schwannoma (VS) surgery. Hypoglossal-facial nerve anastomosis (HFA) is a nerve repair technique used in patients with facial nerve injury. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the techniques, outcomes, and complications of HFA for facial nerve injury following VS resection. A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Herdin databases was conducted from inception to September 2025. Studies were included if they reported HFA for facial nerve injury after VS surgery. Data on patient demographics, interval between injury and HFA, surgical techniques, outcomes, complications, and follow-up duration were obtained. A meta-analysis of comparative studies was performed using RevMan software. Forty-eight studies comprising 866 VS patients were included. The mean age ranged from 35.4 to 56.3 years. The most frequently reported HFA technique was end-to-end, followed by side-to-end, hemihypoglossal-facial anastomosis, and dual nerve transfer (HFA + masseter-facial anastomosis). 91.0% of patients demonstrated improvement in facial function; 46.4% achieved House-Brackmann grade III or better. Meta-analysis conducted on four studies showed significantly greater odds of favorable outcome after HFA versus conservative treatment (OR 6.42, 95% CI 1.74-23.65; p = 0.005). Complications included tongue hemiatrophy (22.5%), eating difficulty (17.0%), synkinesis (14.1%), and speech disarticulation (8.3%). Our review showed that HFA improved the facial nerve function of patients with facial nerve injury after resection of VS, but this procedure carried a notable risk of complications, particularly tongue hemiatrophy.

title: Efficacy of disease-modifying therapies in primary progressive multiple sclerosis: systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS) leads to continuous neurodegeneration. Treatment options are limited, but B-cell-depleting therapies and brain-penetrant Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors have emerged. Compare the efficacy of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) on 12-week composite confirmed disability progression (cCDP12) in PPMS. Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of Phase III randomized trials (up to June 2026). Binomial likelihood models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% credible intervals (CrI). Five trials (4306 patients) were included. Fenebrutinib (OR 0.52, 95% CrI 0.37-0.72; estimated absolute risk reduction [ARR] = 14.1%, number needed to treat [NNT] = 7), standard ocrelizumab 600 mg (OR 0.71, 95% CrI 0.57-0.87; ARR = 7.8%, NNT = 13), and high-dose ocrelizumab (OR 0.65, 95% CrI 0.45-0.94; ARR = 9.6%, NNT = 11) significantly reduced cCDP12 risk versus placebo. Fingolimod was not effective (OR 0.98, 95% CrI 0.73-1.33). In indirect network comparisons under fixed-effects assumptions, fenebrutinib demonstrated lower odds of cCDP12 relative to standard ocrelizumab (OR 0.73, 95% CrI 0.57-0.95), whereas direct head-to-head trial data from FENtrepid demonstrated comparable primary efficacy / non-inferiority. Under a random-effects sensitivity model, credible intervals widened and crossed 1.00 (OR 0.73, 95% CrI 0.40-1.38), reflecting structural uncertainty in a sparse network. Fenebrutinib and ocrelizumab (standard and high-dose) show efficacy in reducing cCDP12 in PPMS. Fenebrutinib demonstrated lower estimated odds of progression under fixed-effects network assumptions, highlighting the clinical potential of central microglial BTK inhibition; however, equivalent direct trial efficacy, loss of statistical significance under random-effects modeling, and baseline clinical heterogeneity (gadolinium-enhancing lesion activity) across trials mandate cautious clinical interpretation. ClinicalTrials.gov: ORATORIO (NCT01194570); ORATORIOHAND (NCT04035005); GAVOTTE (NCT04548999); FENtrepid (NCT04544449); INFORMS (NCT00731692).

title: Rapid turnover of corticosterone in humans.
abstract: Adrenal insufficiency is primarily treated with replacement of cortisol, which is the predominant circulating glucocorticoid. Human adrenals also secrete corticosterone and emerging evidence suggests this may be a safer glucocorticoid replacement therapy. However, there is scant literature describing corticosterone physiology or potential pharmacokinetics in humans. To investigate the secretion and metabolism of corticosterone in comparison with cortisol, we: 1) investigated daytime profiles of circulating cortisol/corticosterone in 7 healthy volunteers; 2) quantified metabolism of both hormones in vitro; 3) measured 24-hour urinary glucocorticoid metabolites in vivo in 24 healthy men; 4) determined the pharmacokinetics of corticosterone during intravenous infusion of 2,2,4,6,6,17α,21,21-[2H]8-corticosterone; and 5) assessed the response of corticosterone and cortisol to 1 μg ACTH in 279 healthy volunteers. Daytime corticosterone profiles closely mirrored those of cortisol, and accounted for ∼3% of total circulating glucocorticoid concentrations. Urinary corticosterone metabolite excretion was approximately 10-fold lower than the corresponding cortisol total, and corticosterone demonstrated substantially faster metabolism by both 5α- and 5β-reductase than cortisol, consistent with its short half-life of 28.5 ± 5.7 minutes. Finally, corticosterone demonstrated a greater proportional response to ACTH than cortisol, particularly in men. Corticosterone and cortisol differ in their metabolism and proportional responses to stimulation. Together with preliminary pharmacokinetic estimates, these data raise the possibility of distinct roles for these two glucocorticoids and inform further physiological and therapeutic investigation.

title: Regenerating Hope: Neural Stem Cell Advances in Combating Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: This review aims to summarize the possible action mechanism, research progress, and clinical transformation trend of Neural Stem Cells (NSCs) in treating ischemic stroke based on current evidence. In this review, PubMed, EMBASE, and Science Direct were systematically searched from inception to 2025 using a combination of subject headings and keywords including "neural stem cells", "ischemic stroke", "cerebral infarction", "mechanism", "signaling pathway", and "clinical trial", with search strategies adapted to each database's specific terminology. The selected literature spans basic and translational research on NSC therapy for ischemic stroke, emphasizing molecular mechanisms. NSC transplantation promotes neural repair through multi-dimensional synergistic mechanisms. Structurally, transplanted NSCs migrate to the infarct area, differentiate into mature neurons and glial cells, and integrate into the host neural network, restoring ultrastructure and the neurovascular unit. Functionally, these changes reduce stroke damage and improve motor and cognitive outcomes, supported by long-term anti-inflammatory, metabolic, and regenerative effects. NSCs secrete trophic factors, such as BDNF and VEGF, that enhance cell survival and repair; recent advances in genetic engineering further enhance their therapeutic efficacy. Early clinical studies confirm NSC therapy safety and show functional recovery. However, significant challenges remain. These include tumorigenicity risk, inconsistent efficacy, and lack of cell source standardization. Addressing these gaps is essential for clinical translation. NSC therapy offers promise for ischemic stroke treatment. Future research must ensure safety, establish standardized protocols, and elucidate mechanisms to facilitate precise clinical application.

title: The Journey to Recovery in Eating Disorders: A Network Analysis Study of Post-Traumatic Growth and Its Psychological Correlates.
journal: European eating disorders review : the journal of the Eating Disorders Association
abstract: Recovery from an eating disorder (ED) is increasingly conceptualised as a multidimensional process that extends beyond symptom remission. Post-traumatic growth (PTG) describes recovery through meaningful changes in broad areas, such as identity and interpersonal relationships. This study investigated facilitators of recovery, PTG and its putative psychological correlates in individuals who self-identified as in recovery from an ED, using network analysis. One-hundred and five participants completed self-report measures of perceived recovery facilitators, PTG, deliberate and intrusive rumination, emotion regulation difficulties, cognitive rigidity, and psychological distress. A regularised partial correlation network was estimated. Expected influence and node predictability were computed. Psychotherapy, social support, and personal motivation were the most endorsed recovery facilitators. Participants reported the greatest improvements in 'interpersonal relationships' (more meaningful and trustful relationships) and 'new possibilities' (new life goals and priorities reorientations). These domains were associated with fewer emotion regulation difficulties and higher deliberate rumination. Cognitive rigidity, difficulties with impulse control under negative emotions and perceived new possibilities showed the highest expected influence and predictability. These findings highlight the relevance of cognitive-emotional processes and future-oriented perspectives to recovery and support broader, person-centred definitions of recovery that encompass personal growth and interpersonal changes alongside symptom remission.

title: Faricimab, a bispecific anti-VEGF/Ang-2 antibody, attenuates ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in a rat model: correlation of ovarian VEGF immunostaining with serum VEGF.
abstract: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a potentially life-threatening complication of assisted reproduction, primarily mediated by increased vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) activity. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of faricimab, a novel bispecific monoclonal antibody, in preventing OHSS in an experimental rat model, and to compare its effects with those of established preventive agents, cabergoline and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists. Thirty-six prepubertal female Wistar albino rats were randomized into six groups: Control, OHSS, OHSS+GnRH antagonist, OHSS + low-dose faricimab, OHSS + high-dose faricimab, and OHSS+cabergoline. OHSS was induced using gonadotropins followed by hCG. Treatments were administered over two days. Ovarian weight, follicle counts, VEGF immunostaining in ovarian tissue, and serum VEGF levels were assessed. A significant difference was found in secondary follicle (p < 0.01), Graafian follicle (p = 0.02), atretic follicle (p = 0.02), and corpus luteum (p = 0.01) counts in low-dose faricimab compared with the OHSS group, with all of these counts significantly lower in the low-dose faricimab group. VEGF staining intensity in ovarian tissue was significantly lower in the OHSS + low-dose faricimab, OHSS+high-dose faricimab, and OHSS+cabergoline groups than the OHSS group (p < 0.01, p < 0.01, and p = 0.04, respectively). Serum VEGF levels were significantly lower in the OHSS + low-dose faricimab, OHSS+high-dose faricimab, and OHSS+cabergoline groups compared with the OHSS group (p < 0.01, p < 0.01, and p = 0.01, respectively). Low-dose faricimab, a novel bispecific monoclonal anti-VEGF antibody, seems to be effective in reducing the risk of OHSS with decreasing VEGF expression in ovarian tissue and serum VEGF levels.

title: Multiscale neural and endocrine control of CD8⁺ T cell fate in cancer: from systemic physiology to local immune circuits.
abstract: CD8⁺ T cells are central cytotoxic effectors of anti-tumor immunity, but tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ populations are functionally heterogeneous and include tumor-reactive, dysfunctional, and bystander states. Although the past decade of cancer immunology has focused largely on how local interactions within the tumor microenvironment shape these states, clinical observations linking chronic stress, sleep disruption, endocrine comorbidity, and circadian timing to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) outcomes indicate that CD8⁺ T cell function is also modulated far beyond the tumor itself. In this review we adopt a whole-organism perspective to examine how autonomic and sensory neural circuits and the endocrine system act across anatomical compartments to govern CD8⁺ T cell priming, trafficking, metabolism, and exhaustion. We first analyze sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory neural axes as systemic effectors mediated by catecholamines, acetylcholine, neuropeptides, and brainstem-driven tone. We then examine endocrine regulation through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, metabolic hormones, and gonadal steroids. We integrate these axes within the tumor microenvironment, where nerve-derived signals, paracrine neuropeptides, and locally amplified glucocorticoid activity form a convergent suppressive network, and at the organismal level through stress amplification loops, sex dimorphism, gut-relayed microbial signaling, and circadian timing. Collectively, this evidence identifies neuro-endocrine signaling as an actionable, mechanistically stratified layer of systemic immune regulation and supports its evaluation as a source of biomarkers and pharmacological targets for sensitizing tumors to ICI therapy. This framework offered here is intended to bridge cancer neuroscience, endocrine oncology, and immunotherapy, and to define the criteria by which the next generation of systems-level immune sensitizers should be evaluated.

title: Spatiotemporally controlled H2S delivery regulates ECM remodeling for osteoarthritis therapy.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint condition marked by gradual breakdown of the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM) within an acidic, oxidative articular microenvironment. Supplementary intervention targeting localized hydrogen sulfide (H2S) deficiency in progressing articular inflammation zones offers a promising therapeutic approach. However, achieving precise control over H2S delivery in terms of both location and timing remains a significant challenge. In this study, we present a core-shell nanoplatform, mPADT@PEG, engineered for dual-responsive H2S release to remodel the ECM. The nanocarrier is activated by the acidic environment within OA lesions, ensuring localized drug accumulation. Additionally, near-infrared (NIR) irradiation triggers H2S release, allowing for precise dose modulation. Mechanistically, spatiotemporal H2S delivery effectively scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), which inhibits the MAPK/p38 signaling pathway, thereby restoring chondrocyte anabolic-catabolic balance and preventing ECM degradation. In vivo experiments in OA models show that this approach reduces inflammation, enhances ECM remodeling, and preserves cartilage integrity. This study demonstrates a precision therapeutic paradigm. Our findings highlight the potential of spatiotemporal H2S modulation as a targeted nanomedicine strategy to slow OA progression.

title: Effect of a multidisciplinary intensive outpatient rehabilitation program on plasma neurofilaments and myokines in Parkinson's disease: an exploratory analysis.
abstract: Physical exercise is increasingly recognized as a supportive intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD), yet the biological mechanisms underlying its effects remain unclear. This study investigated whether exercise-based rehabilitation modulates circulating biomarkers associated with neuroaxonal integrity, inflammation, and muscle-brain communication. In this randomized controlled substudy, 40 PwPD were assigned to a multidisciplinary intensive outpatient rehabilitation program (experimental group, EXP; n = 20) or a home-based self-managed intervention (control group, CTRL; n = 20). Assessments were performed at baseline (T0), post-treatment (T1), and 3-month follow-up (T2). Clinical outcomes included motor function (UPDRS-III), cognition (MoCA), and functional status (ADL, IADL). Plasma levels of neurofilament light chain (NFL), irisin, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and soluble IL-6 receptor (sIL-6R) were measured. No significant changes over time or between groups were observed in motor or cognitive outcomes. In contrast, significant biomarker modulation was detected. Irisin levels increased in the EXP group at T1 and T2, while decreasing in the CTRL group (p < 0.01). NFL levels significantly decreased in the EXP group at both time points, whereas an increase was observed at follow-up in the CTRL group. IL-6 remained stable in both groups. sIL-6R levels decreased over time, with a significant group-by-time interaction at T1 (p = 0.038). No significant correlations emerged between clinical outcomes and biomarkers. Intensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation was associated with significant modulation of circulating biomarkers, despite the absence of clinical changes. Decreased NFL and increased irisin suggest potential neuroprotective and exercise-responsive effects. These findings support the use of plasma biomarkers as sensitive indicators of neurobiological adaptations to rehabilitation in PwPD. Trial registration The original randomized controlled trial (RCT) was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Study ID: NCT05452655).

title: Maternal BMI modulates cord plasma NT-proBNP in gestational diabetes linking cardiac stress to insulin-cortisol crosstalk.
abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is an increasingly prevalent pregnancy disorder associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, including an increased risk of early-onset cardiovascular disease in infants. GDM is associated with cardiac structural and functional changes as early as in utero. However, pathways linking maternal metabolic status to fetal cardiac stress remain poorly defined. We investigated N-teminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) in umbilical cord plasma (UCP) as a candidate biomarker of fetal cardiac stress, together with additional cardiac, endocrine and endothelial biomarkers to identify novel links between fetal cardiac health and maternal and fetal metabolic, inflammatory and hormonal characteristics. UCP from 82 term pregnancies (57 controls, 25 GDM) was analyzed for NT-proBNP and complementary cardiac, endocrine, and endothelial markers. Associations with maternal metabolic parameters, neonatal outcomes, and other UCP parameters were assessed using correlation, regression, and mediation analyses, adjusted for gestational age and neonatal sex. NT-proBNP levels were elevated in the cord plasma of GDM pregnancies, specifically in the presence of increased maternal pre-pregnancy BMI. Across the cohort, NT-proBNP was further associated with maternal BMI at delivery, fasting glucose levels, placental weight, and neonatal C-peptide, while inversely associated with cord plasma cortisol. Mediation analyses identified a significant indirect association involving neonatal C-peptide and suggested a potential mediating role of NT-proBNP in the association between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and cord plasma cortisol. These findings suggest that NT-proBNP may reflect fetal cardiac load in GDM and is associated with maternal metabolic status and fetal insulin secretion. The inverse association between NT-proBNP and cortisol raises the possibility of an interplay between natriuretic peptide signaling and glucocorticoid regulation, pointing towards a potential cardiac-endocrine adaptation to intrauterine metabolic stress. While these observations deserve further investigation, they provide new insights into cardiovascular programming.
keywords: Developmental Origins of Health and Disease

title: Comparative efficacy and safety of silodosin (Silorap®) versus tamsulosin (Tamsolin®) for medical expulsive therapy of distal ureteral stones.
abstract: The study objective was to compare the efficacy and safety of Silodosin (Silorap®) versus Tamsulosin (Tamsolin®) in facilitating the passage of acutely obstructing distal ureteral stones. This multicenter, randomized, comparative study enrolled 336 adult patients with a single distal ureteric calculus (5-10 mm) across sixteen tertiary care centers in Pakistan. Participants were randomized to receive Silodosin (Silorap®) or Tamsulosin (Tamsolin®) and followed for 30 days. Primary outcome was stone expulsion rate at four weeks; secondary outcomes included time to expulsion, analgesic use, emergency visits, and safety outcomes. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. The stone expulsion rate was significantly higher with Silodosin (112/166; 67.47%) than with Tamsulosin (92/170; 54.12%; p = 0.012). Mean expulsion time was 13.68 ± 8.97 days for Silodosin and 14.33 ± 9.65 days for Tamsulosin (median 12 days; p = 0.701). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed similar time to passage (log-rank p = 0.728). Pain scores declined significantly in both groups. Both treatments were well tolerated; headache and postural hypotension were the most common adverse events, while retrograde ejaculation occurred more frequently with Silodosin. Serious events such as palpitation and syncope were rare and manageable, with no significant differences in vital signs. Silodosin (Silorap®) and Tamsulosin (Tamsolin®) are effective and well tolerated for medical expulsive therapy in distal ureteral stones. Silodosin achieved a higher stone expulsion rate, though time to expulsion was similar between groups. ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT05977647; Date of registration: 2023-08-04.

title: Inflammation-associated serum amyloid A amplifies amyloid-β-driven oxidative stress and microglial activation.
abstract: Systemic inflammation is increasingly recognised as a key modifier of Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, yet the mechanisms linking inflammatory acute-phase responses to Amyloid-β (Aβ)-driven neurotoxicity remain incompletely defined. Here, we report that amyloidogenic acute-phase peptide fragment SAA19-45 (SAA27), derived from Serum Amyloid A (SAA), modulates Aβ aggregation and amplifies downstream oxidative and inflammatory stress responses in neuronal and microglial systems.Immunofluorescence analysis of human AD brain tissue revealed plaque-associated SAA-positive cellular structures within or adjacent to Aβ-positive pathological microenvironments across all range of Braak stages. In vitro, co-incubation of SAA27 with Aβ accelerated Thioflavin T-positive aggregation kinetics and altered fibrillar organisation. In SH-SY5Y neurons, Aβ induced marked cytotoxicity and oxidative stress, and SAA27 selectively enhanced intracellular reactive oxygen species without a proportional increase in cell death. In HMC3 microglia, Aβ triggered oxidative stress and inflammatory activation, both of which were further amplified by SAA27, as reflected by increased reactive oxygen species and elevated IL-6 secretion. Similarly, SAA27 enhanced Aβ-induced IL-1β release in monocyte-derived microglia-like cells. In zebrafish larvae, Aβ and SAA27 co-injection produced a stronger ThT-positive amyloid signal and synaptic degeneration, compared with Aβ alone, supporting enhanced amyloid accumulation and synaptic disruption in vivo. Quantitative proteomics revealed Aβ-driven stress and proteostasis-related reprogramming in both neurons and microglia, with SAA27 biasing these responses toward oxidative and activation-associated pathways consistent with microglial remodelling and immune engagement. The polyphenol epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) suppressed fibrillar aggregation in vitro and in zebrafish larvae, preserved synaptic integrity in vivo, attenuated oxidative and inflammatory responses, and differentially modulated cellular proteomic states, promoting near-restoration in neurons while inducing a distinct, less stress-associated state in microglia.Together, these findings identify SAA27 as an inflammation-associated co-factor that accelerates Aβ assembly and amplifies oxidative and innate immune stress responses. The observed partial overlap with human AD proteomic signatures further supports the disease relevance of these pathways. This work provides mechanistic insight into how systemic inflammatory states may exacerbate amyloid-driven neuroinflammation in AD and highlights inflammation-amyloid crosstalk as a pharmacologically modifiable axis.

title: Multimodal data integration for diagnosis and risk prediction of major depressive disorder in the UK Biobank.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) diagnosis currently relies on subjective assessments, limiting early detection and accurate risk stratification. To address this, we developed machine learning models for both prevalent diagnosis and 15-year incident risk prediction using multimodal data from 30,040 UK Biobank participants. We integrated six modalities-proteomics, metabolomics, lifestyle factors, family history, biochemical measures, and polygenic risk scores (PRS)-employing a geographically stratified design with England-based participants for training and those from Scotland and Wales for independent validation. The integrated multimodal model demonstrated superior robustness, yielding a stable mean time-dependent AUC of 0.679 for incident prediction and an AUC of 0.791 for prevalent diagnosis. Crucially, our analysis revealed that modifiable lifestyle factors, particularly sleep patterns, and proteomic profiles consistently outperformed polygenic risk scores, which showed limited independent discriminative ability. Notably, the diagnostic model exhibited high specificity, effectively distinguishing MDD from schizophrenia (AUC = 0.865), bipolar disorder (AUC = 0.799), and anxiety disorders (AUC = 0.729). Feature attribution revealed distinct molecular signatures for disease stages: inflammatory mediators including CTSL and MMP7 dominated diagnosis, whereas markers of neuroplasticity and metabolism such as LRRN1 and LEP emerged as key predictors of future risk. Furthermore, biological enrichment analyses implicated dysregulated immune regulation (specifically neutrophil degranulation), lipid metabolism, and signal transduction pathways, highlighting a potential mechanistic shift from metabolic vulnerability in the risk phase to systemic inflammation in the symptomatic state. These findings demonstrate that integrating multimodal data significantly improves the characterization of MDD, offering a scalable framework for objective biomarker discovery and personalized risk assessment.

title: Comparison of methods to determine platelet reactivity under treatment with aspirin.
abstract: Insufficient response to aspirin is associated with increased cardiovascular risk, but its prognostic relevance in patients receiving potent P2Y12 inhibitors remains uncertain. We assessed methods to identify high on-treatment platelet reactivity (HTPR) under aspirin and evaluated the impact of potent versus less potent P2Y12 inhibition in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Platelet function was analyzed in 757 aspirin-pretreated CAD patients treated with clopidogrel (n = 406), ticagrelor (n = 152), or prasugrel (n = 165). Antiplatelet efficacy was assessed using multiple electrode aggregometry (MEA), platelet function analyzer-100 (PFA-100®), cone and platelet analyzer (CPA), and serum thromboxane B2 (TXB2). All-cause mortality was assessed over five years, and major bleeding and major adverse cardiac events (MACE) over one year. AA-induced MEA > 6 U was associated with higher long-term mortality, however, discriminatory performance was modest (AUC = 0.575, p = 0.051), while CPA-SC < 6% strongly predicted major bleeding (AUC = 0.759, p = 0.001). None of the aspirin-related assays predicted MACE. Prasugrel or ticagrelor treatment was associated with lower long-term mortality than clopidogrel (HR = 0.411; 95% CI: 0.27-0.62; p < 0.001). Concomitant use of potent P2Y12 inhibitors and aspirin resulted in fewer aspirin semi- or non-responders and lower rates of dual HTPR. Dual HTPR occurred in ~ 1% of ticagrelor-, 2% of prasugrel-, and 7% of clopidogrel-treated patients. Exploratory analyses suggested that AA-MEA and CPA-SC were associated with long-term mortality and major bleeding, respectively. Given the modest discriminatory performance of AA-MEA, these findings require external validation. Potent P2Y12 inhibitors reduced dual HTPR, while platelet function assays provided complementary prognostic information in CAD.

title: Neonatal sevoflurane exposures induced cognitive impairment via Satb2-mediated synaptic deficits.
abstract: Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 (Satb2) is a DNA binding protein, and involved in transcription regulation and chromatin remodeling. Studies demonstrated that the absence of Satb2 mediated cognitive impairments in humans and rodents. Moreover, animal research reported that neonatal exposure to sevoflurane induced cognitive dysfunction in adolescent period, along with damage of synaptic plasticity, but the mechanisms are still not clear. Herein, we aimed to determine the role of Satb2 in neurotoxicity caused by sevoflurane. A total of 254 neonatal male Sprague-Dawley rats were used in this study. Neonatal rats were exposed to 30% O2 or 3.0% sevoflurane delivered in 30% O2 for 3 h on postnatal day 7 (P7). Cognitive function was evaluated through open field, Y maze, and novel object recognition tests from P28 to P35. The hippocampi were harvested on P14, P21, and P35. Effects of sevoflurane on Satb2, and synapse in the hippocampus were investigated by western blot, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and Golgi staining. To further screen key molecules, another batch of hippocampi were harvested immediately and 24 h after gas exposure, and subjected to RNA sequencing. Finally, Satb2 overexpression was induced by lentivirus injection into the lateral ventricle on P1, followed by gas exposure on P7. Next, some rats underwent behavioral tests on P28-P35. Hippocampi from another group of rats were harvested on P35 for Western blot, qRT-PCR, and Golgi staining. Y maze test showed that sevoflurane reduced the spontaneous alternation ratio in young rats. Novel object recognition test also revealed that sevoflurane decreased recognition index, the entries, and duration in novel arm, along with prolonged the latency to novel arm. Persistent decrease in Satb2, postsynaptic density protein-95 (PSD95), and spine density were observed. Moreover, RNA sequencing also revealed the decrease in Satb2 mRNA caused by neonatal exposure to sevoflurane. Furthermore, we found that lentivirus (LV)-induced Satb2 overexpression partially restored the decreases in the PSD95, spine density, spontaneous alternation ratio, recognition index, the entries, and duration in novel arm, and the increase in latency to novel arm caused by sevoflurane exposure. These results suggest that decreased Satb2 may contribute to cognitive disorders by reducing PSD95 levels, resulting in synaptic deficits. Meanwhile, this emphasizes that Satb2 was a potential target to intervening cognitive impairment caused by sevoflurane exposure.

title: Loss of M1 acetylcholine receptor-mediated orexinergic activity contributes to immune dysfunction in experimental sepsis.
abstract: Sepsis is a lethal syndrome caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The brain's contribution to sepsis pathogenesis is understudied. We previously demonstrated that cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) reduced activity in the orexinergic nervous system and altered physiologic, endocrine and immune variables; changes were attenuated by intrathecal injection of orexin or by administration of the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (M1mAChR) agonist xanomeline. We hypothesize that CLP-induced changes resulted from an interaction between orexinergic neurons and M1-mediated activities. We studied CLP effects on 1) wild type (WT) mice, 2) transgenic mice (TGs) whose orexinergic neurons were chemogenetically activated, 3) WTs given xanomeline and 4) WTs given xanomeline and almorexant, a non-specific orexin antagonist that crosses the blood-brain Barrier. After periodically recording vital signs we euthanized mice at 48 h post-CLP, harvested, fixed and immunostained hypothalamic/forebrain sections. We measured plasma levels of hormones and cytokines and characterized splenic cell phenotypes using flow cytometry. Significance was determined using ANOVA with Tukey's correction. CLP reduced vital signs and hormone levels and elevated levels of several cytokines/chemokines. Xanomeline administration reversed CLP-induced decreases in orexinergic activity. In contrast, chemogenetic orexinergic re-activation in TGs did not affect CLP-induced decreases in activity in basal forebrain cholinergic neurons. Chemogenetically restoring orexinergic activity or administering xanomeline reversed CLP-induced changes in vital signs and in levels of hormones and of TNFα, MIP-1α, MCP-1 and IL-1β; almorexant reversed xanomeline effects on TNFα, MIP-1α and MCP-1 but not on IL-1β. Orexinergic re-activation, but not xanomeline, attenuated CLP-induced IL-6, IL-10 and CXCL1 elevations. Both orexinergic re-activation in TGs and xanomeline administration to WTs reversed CLP-induced increases in numbers of splenic innate immune cells; xanomeline effects were not altered by almorexant. Other CLP-associated effects on splenic cells were unaltered. CLP-induced changes in vital signs and hormones. TNFα, MIP-1α and MCP-1 levels reflect attenuated M1-stimulated orexinergic activity. CLP-induced elevations of IL-6, IL-10 and CXCL1 levels involved a pathway that reduced orexinergic activity but did not involve M1mAChRs. Decreased orexinergic and M1-mediated activity independently contributed to CLP-induced changes in IL-1β levels and in splenic cell numbers.

title: Increase in IgM Autoantibodies to Aβ1-42 in Plasma of Men with Alzheimer's disease.
journal: Doklady biological sciences : proceedings of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR, Biological sciences sections
abstract: The pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with impaired metabolism of the beta‑amyloid peptide (Aβ), which acts not only as a pathogenetically significant factor but also as a potential autoantigen capable of inducing a humoral immune response. In contrast to IgG antibodies to Aβ, which have been studied quite extensively, the levels of IgM antibodies to this peptide in AD patients and healthy donors remain poorly investigated. In the present study, we performed a comparative evaluation of IgM titers to Aβ1-42 in the peripheral blood plasma of 26 AD patients and 26 healthy donors using enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The obtained data demonstrate a statistically significant elevation of IgM antibody titers to Aβ1-42 in the plasma of men with AD compared to the healthy donor group.

title: Comparison of five definitions of meaningful change on patient-reported outcomes in four SWOG clinical trials.
abstract: The minimally important difference (MID) represents how much change on a patient-reported outcome (PRO) is considered meaningful for defining a patient as improving or worsening. MIDs can be based on a statistical distribution or anchored to another PRO. This study used four SWOG clinical trials with treatments of known toxicities and positive quality of life (QOL) results as a silver standard to compare different MID definitions. Two breast cancer trials compared true acupuncture (S1200) to sham acupuncture and waitlist control or duloxetine (S1202) to placebo to improve pain. S9346 compared continuous versus intermittent androgen deprivation therapy in metastatic prostate cancer. S1404 compared pembrolizumab with physician's choice of interferon or ipilimumab in melanoma. Four MID distribution definitions (30% change, 50% change, half a standard deviation (0.5SD), reliable change index (RCI)) and one MID prospective anchor-based definition were compared. Chi-square statistics for intervention effect compared different definitions of MID. In S1200, the 0.5SD and RCI performed the best with the anchor-based method also performing well. In S1202, the anchor method, 0.5SD and 50% change performed well. For S9346, the anchor method performed well in physical function comparisons. For S1404, RCI and 30% change performed well for worsening QOL. Across all comparisons, 0.5SD had the highest mean chi-square values for worsening symptoms and RCI had the highest mean chi-square values for improvement. Results suggest that some distribution-based MID methods may be sensitive to change for symptom and QOL PROs. Anchor-based methods may be the most sensitive for function PROs.

title: A dual-readout visual immunosensor based on multicolor and test line counting modes for fenitrothion detection.
abstract: A novel dual-readout visual immunosensor was constructed that combines multicolor chromogenic and test line (T-Line) counting modalities for the sensitive and instrument-free detection of fenitrothion. A nanobody-alkaline phosphatase fusion protein (VHHjd8-ALP) was adopted as the signal reporter in a one-step competitive immunoassay format. In the multicolor mode, Prussian blue (PB) nanocubes acted as both a peroxidase-mimicking nanozyme and a colorimetric probe, enabling a visible color transition (blue-green-yellow) in response to increasing fenitrothion concentrations, with a limit of detection (LOD, IC10) of 16.6 ng/mL. In the T-Line counting mode, MnO2@BSA nanoneedles were immobilized on nitrocellulose (NC) membranes to form five T-Lines, which were sequentially etched by ascorbic acid (AA) generated from VHHjd8-ALP. This semiquantitative mode offered an LOD of 1.95 ng/mL and allowed naked-eye readout by counting the remaining T-Lines. Both modes were validated in spiked food samples (cucumber, Chinese cabbage, and apple), showing recoveries of 80.0-111.0% and high consistency with GC-MS/MS results. The proposed dual-readout immunosensor provides a simple, low-cost, and user-friendly platform for on-site screening of fenitrothion, with distinct advantages in sensitivity and visual interpretability.

title: Recommendations on key aspects of migraine prevention: A Delphi consensus among experts of the headache study group of the Spanish society of neurology (GECSEN).
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: This study presents a Delphi consensus developed by the Headache Study Group of the Spanish Society of Neurology (GECSEN) to establish updated recommendations on key aspects of preventive migraine management. Given the high global burden of migraine and the emergence of novel preventive therapies-particularly OnabotulinumtoxinA and Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-targeted treatments-there is a need to redefine therapeutic goals and optimize clinical decision-making. A nine-member Steering Committee defined 14 statements addressing five domains: candidate patient selection, therapeutic goals, treatment discontinuation, switching strategies, and combination therapy. A systematized literature review (171 selected publications) informed statement development. Eighty-eight migraine specialists participated in the first Delphi round and 48 in the second. Consensus was determined using the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method. Agreement was achieved for all 14 recommendations after two voting rounds. Preventive therapy is recommended in patients with ≥ 4 monthly migraine or moderate-to-severe headache days and relevant quality-of-life impairment. The ideal therapeutic goal is migraine freedom or minimization of attack frequency and intensity with improved quality of life. Optimal control is defined as < 4 monthly moderateto-severe headache days within three months. Treatment should generally be maintained for at least 12 months after achieving optimal control. Switching or combining preventive therapies-including CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants, and OnabotulinumtoxinA-may be considered in insufficient responders. This consensus proposes a treat-to-target strategy centered on patient-reported outcomes and residual disease burden, aiming to standardize preventive migraine care and improve long-term clinical outcomes.

title: Spectral power and functional connectivity alterations in multiple system atrophy revealed by resting-state EEG.
abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is an aggressive α-synucleinopathy characterized by motor and autonomic dysfunction. Elucidating neurophysiological patterns can provide crucial insights into the underlying neural mechanisms. Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and fMRI data were collected from 69 healthy controls and 123 MSA patients, comprising a discovery cohort (n = 97) and an independent validation cohort (n = 26). MSA patients showed reduced delta power in the cerebellar, frontoparietal, visual I, and limbic networks, with widespread increases in theta and high gamma power. Amplitude-based connectivity decreased across the alpha, beta, and gamma bands in subcortical, cerebellar, default mode, motor, and visual I networks, with increased theta-band synchrony involving motor, visual II, and frontoparietal networks. These EEG abnormalities were corroborated by fMRI connectivity, highlighting cross-modal consistency. Canonical correlation analysis revealed associations between EEG features and motor/non-motor symptom severity. Interpretable stacking models accurately classified MSA-C and MSA-P subtypes and predicted UMSARS progression in longitudinal follow-up. These findings identified aberrant neural activity and network dysfunction in MSA, highlighting EEG as a promising biomarker for disease monitoring.

title: The Neurocardiac Axis in Myocardial Infarction: Emerging Role of Brain-Heart Inflammatory Signaling.
abstract: Myocardial infarctions (MI) can lead to post-MI cardiac and neurocognitive dysfunctions due to the complex interplay of the neurocardiac "brain and heart" axis. Imbalanced autonomic nervous system (ANS) synchronization within the neurocardiac axis leads to infarcted or damaged tissues. This may influence potential inflammatory signaling mechanisms in post-MI pathology and, by extension, the repercussions of acute and chronic MI outcomes. Here, previous in-vivo experimental rodent and porcine models with surgically induced MI/heart failure (HF) and in-vitro models report brain-heart association regions and pathologies. Furthermore, clinical meta-analyses were compiled to provide a broad overview of the varying impacts of post-MI pathologies on the brain and heart. Other supplemental perspectives postulate other relevant inflammatory mechanisms, such as neurohumoral imbalances, a weakened immune system, and genetic predispositions, which expand a more holistic view of post-MI mechanisms. By examining in closer detail the inflammatory cells (e.g., microglia and astrocytes) and the blood-brain barrier (BBB), cardiogenic trauma from MI incites chronic systemic inflammation and exacerbates the stress response. This further weakens the BBB, prolongs neuroinflammation, and damages sites responsible for cardiac regulation and repair.

title: Brain penetration of benserazide inversely associates with levodopa response in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Levodopa combined with a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor (DDCI) is the first-line treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD), yet interindividual response variability remains poorly understood.
